intro: In the Romanza (Moderato) from Elgar’s Variations on an Original Theme “Enigma”, Op. 36, a clarinet quotes Mendelssohn’s Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage over the throb of a liner’s engines. Elgar put three asterisks in place of his traveller’s name.

sections.label: Var 13 · Romanza, Moderato, clarinet over strings
sections.mNote: The Romanza begins in G major.

sections.label: Quotation · Mendelssohn quotation, solo clarinet
sections.mNote: Solo clarinet above a soft timpani roll.

sections.label: Var 13 · Brass, then Romanza theme
sections.mNote: A short brass swell; the clarinet then returns.

cues.title: Clarinet melody, Moderato in G major
cues.text: A clarinet plays the melody over rising and falling lines in the second violins and cellos. The first violins join, and the winds then extend the phrase. Elgar called this a Romanza; it opens Moderato in G major.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 87, rehearsal 55: Moderato in G major, opening clarinet melody and moving second-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinet quotation of Mendelssohn
cues.text: The clarinet quotes Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage by Mendelssohn over a timpani roll marked ppp. Elgar asks for side-drum sticks on the timpani. In his commentary he identified the sound beneath the tune as the engines of a distant liner.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 88, rehearsal 56: tranquillo, quotation marks around the clarinet phrase and timpani marked ppp with side-drum sticks. Elgar’s account of the liner appears at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, variation XIII.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lady Mary Lygon
cues.text: Lady Mary Lygon of Madresfield Court, the probable subject, supported local music-making and sailed to Australia in 1899. Her initials, L.M.L., appear in Elgar’s sketches. In print, three asterisks replace them, and in the variation the clarinet plays a borrowed tune.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society regards Lady Mary Lygon as the probable subject: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm. Her festival support and the initials L.M.L. in the sketches are discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, citing Michael Kennedy, Portrait of Elgar, pp. 95–96. Helen Weaver is an alternative identification; the voyage began after the music was completed.

transitions.title: The clarinet’s Mendelssohn quotation
transitions.from: Var 13 · Romanza, Moderato, clarinet over strings
transitions.how: Poco rallentando leads to tranquillo at rehearsal 56. The upper strings fade out while divided violas keep a small rising-and-falling figure moving. A soft timpani roll and held cello notes support the clarinet’s Mendelssohn quotation. The score puts quotation marks around the borrowed phrase.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 88, rehearsal 56: slowing, divided viola accompaniment, soft timpani, held cellos and the marked clarinet quotation.

transitions.title: Brass crescendo before Come prima
transitions.how: Trumpets, trombones and tuba enter softly and then make a crescendo over repeated figures in the low strings. The timpani change from a roll to measured notes. The brass soon drop away at the diminuendo molto. At Come prima the clarinet and the moving strings of the G major Romanza return.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 90, rehearsals 58–59: brass crescendo over repeating low strings, measured timpani notes, diminuendo molto and Come prima.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 87–92, rehearsal figures 55–60: the clarinet Romanza, quotations from Mendelssohn and the central brass passage.

timeline.note: Clarinet plays over rocking second violins and cellos (p. 87).
Winds and strings take up the Romanza phrase, with quiet horn chords beneath them (p. 87).
Solo clarinet quotes Mendelssohn above a soft timpani roll and quiet strings (p. 88).
The clarinet continues over rocking violas and a held cello note (p. 89).
Brass chords swell and recede above the timpani before the Romanza returns (p. 90).
Marked Come prima, the Romanza returns to the woodwinds and rocking strings (pp. 90–91).
The strings stop and the timpani roll returns beneath another clarinet quotation (p. 92).
Clarinet, violas and cellos remain after the upper strings, horns and basses fall silent (p. 92).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
